A1.justification: Both PDFs describe AMA-Bench and AMA-Agent. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching relocated appendix material.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations on real-world and synthetic trajectories, memory-component ablations, and human validation of its automated judge.

after.justification: v3 retains those original results and adds downstream task evaluations, efficiency measurements, judge comparisons, and LoCoMo evaluation.

M1.justification: The graph-and-tool architecture remains, but the reported prompts change substantively. Appendix D in v1 becomes Appendix K in v3: construction now requests key-turn state-memory compression with verbatim preservation, and retrieval explicitly forces counting and aggregation queries to code execution. These revise component behavior within the existing architecture.

E1.justification: v3 adds actual evaluation on dialogue-memory benchmark LoCoMo, previously only discussed as related work. It also adds interactive task completion on TextWorld and Spider2, extending evaluation beyond answering questions about recorded trajectories. The original six real-world domains and two synthetic environments remain.

E2.justification: Table 5 adds evaluated HiMem and EMem rows while retaining the existing comparators. Other added analyses primarily reuse existing comparison methods; HippoRAG and HippoRAG2 naming variations do not establish an additional comparator.

E3.justification: New protocols include controlled interactive execution with a fixed Qwen3-32B agent, task-success and latency measurements, difficulty-stratified evaluation, four alternative judges, and GPT-5-mini-backed synthetic evaluation. Additional audits sample 720 QA pairs for evidence analysis and 200 for tool usage. The original main-evaluation settings remain; the newly explicit independent, fixed-memory QA protocol is a disclosure.

E4.justification: v3 adds substantial analyses of whether QA predicts task success, how difficulty affects completion, latency versus accuracy, sensitivity to backbone and judge, evidence positions and multi-hop requirements, and selective tool usage. It also adds qualitative TextWorld behavior comparisons. The original component ablations and Mem0 extraction case study are retained.

E5.justification: Section 6.3 newly specifies Pearson correlation estimation across six memory systems for QA accuracy versus task success, whereas v1 presents qualitative rank alignment in Figure 9. Neither version reports repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, or significance tests for the benchmark comparisons.

E6.justification: The original main-table scores remain, including AMA-Agent's 0.5722 average. Added results include HiMem at 0.2995 and EMem at 0.4610 in Table 5, downstream success in Table 6, LoCoMo accuracy of 76.20% in Table 23, and extensive diagnostic measurements. Table 22 additionally gives unexplained Qwen3-32B averages differing from Table 5, so these cannot establish a reliable same-setting performance change.

T1.justification: The POMDP formulation and Build/Retrieve definitions remain unchanged, as does the relocated needle-generation algorithm. The added fixed-memory QA equation clarifies evaluation using the existing framework; it introduces no substantive theoretical result, assumption, or proof.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same benchmark contribution, memory-design bottleneck claim, graph-and-tool solution, and headline 57.22% accuracy and 11.16% advantage. Added evaluations expand supporting evidence without redefining these central contributions.

C2.justification: v3 adds interpretations concerning localized extraction errors, selective tool overhead, downstream validity of QA, efficiency, cross-model robustness, and generalization beyond agent trajectories. Some interpretations exceed the tables: Appendix I claims preserved comparator ordering and a widening advantage, although Table 22 supports neither consistently. The existing in-episode-memory limitation remains.

D1.justification: v3 explicitly documents independent open-ended queries against fixed constructed memory and revises all three implementation prompts, including state-memory schemas and the code-output result variable. Existing baseline configurations remain substantially unchanged. The added HiMem and EMem comparisons receive no corresponding implementation recipes.

R1.justification: v3 adds HiMem and EMem citations and positions its results against these recent memory systems. Both references remain Anonymous entries with TODO citation placeholders. The broader related-work taxonomy is unchanged; the Du et al. title update refers to the same cited work.

P1.justification: Most existing prose is retained. Changes include focused explanations in Sections 5–6, a Further Analyses subsection, rewritten prompt templates, and appendix reordering that moves prompts and dataset examples to K and L. Author affiliation, conference information, and running headers are also updated.

P2.justification: v3 substantially expands the table presentation with downstream-performance, evidence-distribution, judge-agreement, efficiency, difficulty, behavior, backbone, and LoCoMo displays, and adds rows to Table 5. Existing figures are retained, with several relocated; the original ablation table becomes Table 7.

improvement.justification: The downstream validation, efficiency analysis, and broader robustness checks address important gaps in v1. However, v3 reports TextWorld success as 51.5% in Table 6 and 50.5% in Table 19, gives conflicting same-described-setting averages in Tables 5 and 22, and makes ranking claims contradicted by Table 22. Incomplete new baseline references further limit verification. These reporting problems materially weaken the added evidence, preventing a reliable judgment of net overall improvement.
